column3: Ishnu-alah, thero'shan. Good fortune to you, honoured student. Let's walk gently today.
Elune-adore. Elune be with you. Wherever today takes you, I'll be close.
Welcome back. The forest kept growing while you were away. Shall we go and see what changed?
A new place. Before the road pulls you on, perhaps look at it properly, once.
Every land has its own quiet. Hear how this one sounds, if you like.
The trees here have stood a long time. They don't mind waiting while you look around.
New ground. Somewhere in it is a view nobody's shown you yet.
The White Lady is watching. The kaldorei say she keeps watch over the world while it sleeps.
Kaldorei. Children of the stars. Our people took their name from the night sky. It's yours to look at, whenever you like.
Night is not the absence of light. It's the time for a gentler one.
The White Lady and the Blue Child, crossing the sky together. Even the moons keep each other company.
You've stopped. Good. Perhaps a slow breath in, and a slower one out. Let your shoulders fall, if they want to.
Nothing to do right now. Only the breath going in, and the breath going out, and the leaves moving.
Three things you can hear, if you listen. Wind, water, something small in the grass. Stay with them a moment.
The druids say you don't have to do anything to be part of the forest. You only have to stay still long enough to notice it.
Feel where you're standing. The ground is holding you up. It always has.
Try letting each breath out last a little longer than the breath in. Once more. The forest is breathing with you.
A roof, a hearth, and a little quiet. Sit for a while. Elune-adore.
Rest is part of the path, not a break from it. Even the oaks sleep through winter.
You're safe here. Let the day settle.
Let the wind carry you. From up here, the roads you worried over look like threads.
Look down, if you like. Every place you've walked is one small part of a much bigger world.
The hippogryph knows the way. You don't have to steer. Just watch.
Forests, rivers, roads. All of it, still there tomorrow. Enjoy the view.
The first kaldorei made their home beside the Well of Eternity. Water has always been where our people gathered.
Let the water hold you up. You don't have to swim hard. Float, for a breath.
Shh. It's all right. When a night elf falls, they walk on as a wisp, a little light in the dark. Find your way back slowly.
Ande'thoras-ethil. May your troubles be diminished. The path home is long, but it's always there.
Falling is part of every journey. Nothing you've learned is lost. Walk back gently.
Another ring on the tree. Perhaps take a moment to notice how far the road has come.
Another step on the path, thero'shan. I was glad to walk it with you.
The oak grows one ring at a time, and never in a hurry.
Andu-falah-dor. Let balance be restored. Come, the day is young.
Stand still a moment, if you like. Let this place learn your footsteps before you learn its roads.
The kaldorei kept their vigil under these same stars. You're keeping it with them now.
Moonlight on the leaves. Nothing needs doing. Just look.
Let your eyes go soft, if you like. Nothing in particular to look at. Only the light coming in.
If your jaw's tight, let it go. Shoulders too. The world can wait a breath.
Warm hands, a full belly, somewhere to sit. The old druids would call that a good day.
Moonwells hold Elune's light the way a cup holds water. Rest beside one, if you pass it.
Rest a moment in the quiet. The spirit healer has seen a thousand travellers find their way back.
Like a sapling turning to the light, another season of growth. Gently does it.
The kaldorei believed Elune slept in the waters of the Well by day, and woke with the night. You may rest too. Rest was never something you had to earn.
Shadowglen. Where so many kaldorei first open their eyes. Everything here is young, and in a way, so are you.
Aldrassil. A tree that holds a whole village in its arms. If you like, rest a hand on the bark as you pass.
Dolanaar. Lanterns, a moonwell, and kaldorei going about their evening. This is what peace looks like when it's ordinary.
Lake Al'Ameth. Still water, and the sky in it twice. Stay a moment, if you'd like, and let the water do the looking.
The Pools of Arlithrien. Quiet water under old trees. Some places ask you to lower your voice. This is one.
Oracle Glade. Old places have long memories. You don't need to understand them to be welcome.
A barrow den. Druids once slept beneath the earth in places like this, dreaming the world well. Tread softly.
Rut'theran. The roots of Teldrassil reach the sea here. Every journey out of the forest begins at its feet.
Darnassus. High in the branches of Teldrassil, the World Tree's own city. Lanterns, water, and nobody in a hurry.
The Temple of the Moon. The Sisters of Elune keep their vigil here. You don't need to pray. Just listen to the water.
The Cenarion Enclave. Every druid here was once a student who didn't yet know their own shape. You're among kin.
Auberdine. Sea wind, and boats waiting at the pier. The wide world is just over that water.
Bashal'Aran. The Highborne lived here once, and loved the Well's magic more than anything. Hunger is a hard master. Pity them, if you can.
Ameth'Aran. Ruins, and restless spirits. Not everything broken here was wicked. Some of it was only lost.
The Grove of the Ancients. They were old before the first city rose. Under branches like these, a worry looks very short.
Astranaar. The Sentinels keep watch so others can sleep. There's a quiet kind of love in that.
Ashenvale. The oldest forest our people know. Look up, if you like. The canopy has been growing for longer than anyone remembers.
Moonglade. The druids' sanctuary, open to anyone who comes in peace. Here, nobody needs to be on guard.
Nighthaven. Lantern light on the lake, and nothing at all to hurry for.
Felwood. This forest is wounded, not wicked. Every tree here would grow green again, given the chance.
The Emerald Sanctuary. Druids, staying in a wounded forest to heal it, one tree at a time. That's what devotion looks like.
Jaedenar. Something sacred was taken here and turned. It isn't yours to carry. Only to set right, a little, if you choose.
Winterspring. Snow under starlight, and air so clean it almost rings. Take a long breath of it, if you like.
Starfall Village. Kaldorei, living in the cold and the quiet. Kin can be found at every edge of the world.
Feathermoon Stronghold. The Sentinels' island home. Strength that stands guard, and asks nothing back.
Felwood again. Grief for a place is a kind of love. Let it be what it is.
The sickness is in the land, not in you. You can walk through it and still be whole.
Every cleansed moonwell here was someone's patient work. Small mending still counts.
Home. The branches hold the moonlight here like a cupped hand.
Back among the kaldorei. Belonging doesn't have to be earned, thero'shan. It's simply yours.
Darnassus. Somewhere, a Sentinel is trading stories with a priestess. Life goes on, gently, while you're away.
Ishnu-dal-dieb. Good fortune to your family. Kin can be chosen, and for a while, these ones are yours.
Tyrande raised Shandris as her own, and Shandris grew up to lead the Sentinels. Family is something you make, too.
Companions. Even the Sentinels keep watch in pairs.
Travel well together. The road is kinder with someone beside you.
Every shan'do was once a thero'shan. Learning from someone is an honour, not a lessening.
A good teacher wants you to need them less. Take what they offer, and make it yours.
Malfurion himself was Cenarius's student. There's no shame in being early on the path.
The bear. Strength that protects, not strength that dominates. Wear it gently.
The seal's shape. The water was never your enemy. Now it's your road.
The cat. Quiet paws, patience, and knowing when to wait. The forest teaches all three.
Swift as a stag. Go far, if you like, but there's no prize for arriving first.
The moonkin. Elune's light, given feathers and a heartbeat.
Rebirth. You can call someone back from death now. A gift worth giving freely.
Moonglade, whenever you need it. A sanctuary is only a thought away now.
Tranquility. The rarest thing a druid can give: calm, poured out over everyone near you.
The storm is part of nature too. Even fury can be held with care.
A stranger, blessed in passing. Kindness like that travels further than you'll ever see.
Help for someone who may never know your name. The forest does that every day, too.
Small mercies, freely given. Whoever receives one tends to pass it on.
That's been hard. It's all right to feel worn down by it. Perhaps rest a while; the grove will wait.
Setbacks are part of every path. Andu-falah-dor. Balance comes back, a little at a time.
Nothing here is lost that can't be found again. If you like, step back, eat, rest, and then decide.
Linger on this a moment. Something's finished, and it went well.
Before the next thing, notice this one. A small task, done with care.
There. Let that settle before you move on. The next road will keep.
A good moment. They're easy to walk straight past.
Dawn. The White Lady hands the sky to the sun, and the forest wakes up yawning.
First light. Night elves rest now, mostly. You may too, if the night's been long.
Dusk. The kaldorei day is beginning. Listen. The forest changes its voice.
The sun's going down. Our hours are coming. Elune-adore.
The night's grown very deep, thero'shan. Even Sentinels hand over the watch. The roads will keep until you've slept.
It's late, even by kaldorei reckoning. Tomorrow's walk will be kinder after some rest.
You've walked a long way today. Is there someone you'd like to share the road with? A word to a friend is a kind of shelter.
A long journey. Perhaps stretch, drink some water, and look at something far away for a moment.
Seventy-five in herbalism. The plants are starting to recognise your hands.
A hundred and fifty. Meadows, hillsides and riverbanks have all passed through your fingers.
Two hundred and twenty-five. You know the herbs by their scent now, and they know you.
Three hundred. An artisan of growing things. And every herb you ever picked grew back.
Seventy-five in skinning. Every hide is a life given. You're learning to waste nothing.
A hundred and fifty. Careful, respectful work. The beasts deserved that, and got it.
Two hundred and twenty-five. A steady knife, and steady thanks.
Three hundred. A master's hands, and still a grateful heart.
Patience got you here. One step, then another, and no hurry in any of them.
You took care on the way, of the land and the people in it. That counts for more than the number.
Curiosity is a strength too. You kept stopping to look, and the world kept answering.
Shadowmeld. The forest folds around you, and for a while, nobody needs anything from you.
Hidden in plain sight, as our people always have been. Stay as long as you like.
Still as a Sentinel on watch. Only, just now, there's nothing to watch for. Let the sounds come to you.
The Dream is close here. The druids who slept in these dens walked it for years. A little while is plenty.
Rest, if you'd like. The world is green and slow on the other side of sleep, and nothing there needs fixing.
The Emerald Dream. The world as it might have been, untouched. Wake whenever you're ready.
Elune-adore. She doesn't ask for words. Kneeling under her light is enough.
The White Lady's light is on your shoulders. Whatever you've carried today, you can set it down here for a while.
The moon wanes, and comes back whole. Every time. Elune-adore.
Before the road starts again, a look back at the last one.
Ishnu-alah. Here's what your last walk held, before the new one begins.
The last journey, in a few words. Let it settle before today's begins.
Rest well, thero'shan. The forest will be here.
Elune-adore. Sleep under her light.
Ishnu-alah. Until the next road.
The Lunar Festival. The druids of Moonglade fill the sky with fireworks, and the Elders are honoured for their wisdom. Look up tonight, if you can.
The Lunar Festival. Nighthaven's lanterns are lit, and Moonglade is full of guests. Every people's old and wise ones are honoured this week.
The Harvest Festival. Tables full, fields gathered in, and the heroes of old remembered. The bread is still warm.
Harvest time. Every herb you've gathered this year was part of it. Eat well, and share.
The Feast of Winter Veil. Snow, lanterns, and gifts left for strangers. Kindness, wrapped in paper.
Hallow's End. Candles in carved faces, and sweets for anyone brave enough to knock. Even the dark can be played with.
The Midsummer Fire Festival. Bonfires on every hill, and the shortest night of the year. For the kaldorei, that's a small sacrifice.
Children's Week. The cities are full of small adventurers, and anyone can spend a day showing one of them something wonderful. Wonder is easy to share.
A week for play. Sweets, small adventures, and someone with time to listen. That kind of care can come from anyone, at any age.
Some of us grew up without the ones who should have held us. If that's you, you're far from alone, and no less a child of the stars.
The kaldorei say some of their dead stay on as wisps, small lights tending the forest. Whatever we do with grief, love that was given doesn't vanish. It lives on in what it grew.
Shandris wasn't born to Tyrande. She was raised by her, and grew strong in that care. Hearts keep learning what safety feels like, from whoever offers it, at any age.
If an old ache stirs, you might speak to it the way I speak to you. Gently, and without hurry. That voice can become your own.
Grief comes and goes, like the tide at Rut'theran. It's all right to feel it, and all right to set it down for a while and simply walk.
Healing is mostly made of ordinary things. Warm food, a friend's voice, sleep, the forest. They add up, slowly, like rings in a tree.
Ande'thoras-ethil. May your troubles be diminished. Old wounds do soften, given care and time. The forest has seen it happen many times.
Children's Week. If it stirs something old, that's all right. Whatever wasn't given back then, care can still be given now, by friends, by the forest, and by you, to yourself.
Shadowmeld. The kaldorei learned to be still as the forest itself. Let the breath come and go on its own for a while.
In the shadow, nobody's looking. There's nothing to do and no one to be. Only this breath, and the next.
Hidden, and safe. If you like, follow the wind as it rises and falls. The light at the edges will breathe with you.
There. The breath has done its work. Stay as long as you like, and step out when you're ready.
Elune-adore. Whatever you brought into the shadow, you can leave a little of it here.
The forest kept watch while you rested. It always will.
Slower now, and steadier. Carry a little of this stillness with you.
Nothing given in this forest is lost, thero'shan. The leaf falls to feed the root, and the root raises the leaf. What you poured out will return to you, changed, and the same.
Ishnu-alah, thero'shan. Welcome. Let's rest in the Dream together for a while. There's nothing to do well here. You only have to arrive, just as you are.
Your eyes can close, or soften, and rest on something low and still. Whichever feels kinder. And if anything feels wrong, simply move, and we'll come back. You're always free to.
Let yourself settle. Let the chair take your weight, and the floor take the chair. You don't have to hold yourself up just now. It's being done for you.
Listen for the furthest sound you can hear, out beyond your room. No need to name it. Just let it be there.
And now the nearest sound. Perhaps your own breath. Perhaps nothing at all. Quiet is welcome too.
Let your shoulders soften, if they'd like to. Your jaw. The small place between your eyebrows. Nothing to force. Only an invitation.
Now the breath, whenever you're ready. Let it come in on its own, and leave a little more slowly than it came.
In, as the wind rises. Out, longer and softer, as it falls.
If your mind wanders, that's alright. Minds wander. Each time you notice and come back, that's the practice, and you're doing it.
Once, only if you'd like: breathe in, then one more small sip of air on top. And let it all go, slowly, like a long sigh.
You can let the breath find its own pace now. It knows the way.

The druids say the Emerald Dream is the world as it would be, left to grow on its own. Picture a clearing there, if you like. Soft moss underfoot. Cool night air. Moonlight through tall trees. A silver moth landing on your hand, gentle and forgiving, like the breeze.
Tall grass, moving in a gentle wind. Somewhere close, still water, holding the stars. Everything here grows at its own pace, and so can you.
Nothing grows faster for being pulled. With each breath out, let something in you settle, the way leaves settle on still water.
Nothing to fix here. Nothing to earn. You're allowed to simply rest.
If it's welcome, a few words for yourself. Perhaps: may I be at ease. May I be gentle with myself. Or whatever words fit better.
You've carried a great deal to get here. It's alright to set some of it down, just for now. It will keep.
And a kind wish for someone else out there today. Someone you know, or someone you'll never meet. May they rest too. Everyone is carrying something.
Rest here a little longer. I'll keep watch.
And now, just listen. The water's edge is waking around you. Frogs, singing the day gently closed. Stay with them as long as you like.
Slowly now, whenever you're ready, come back towards waking. Feel your hands. Perhaps move your fingers, and your shoulders.
When you'd like to, open your eyes. Look around, and find one thing you can see.
Andu-falah-dor, thero'shan. Balance restored, a little. That was well done. The Dream will keep. So will I.
Ishnu-alah, thero'shan. Come, let's walk into the Dream together for a little while. Eight minutes or so. Close your eyes, or let them rest on something low and still. Whichever feels kinder.
If anything feels wrong at any point, simply move, and we'll come back. You're always free to.
Let the waking world go quiet. Listen for the furthest sound in your own room. And then the nearest one.
Notice what's holding you up. The chair, the floor beneath it. You don't have to hold yourself up just now. It's being done for you.
Now the breath, if you like. Nothing to force. Let it come in on its own, and leave a little more slowly than it came.
In, as the wind rises. Out, longer, as it falls. Let the breath out be the longest part.
If your mind wanders, that's what minds do. Noticing is the practice. Come back to the wind, gently, as many times as it takes.
Once, if you'd like: breathe in, then take one more small sip of air on top. And let it all go, slowly.

The druids say the Emerald Dream is the world as it would be, left to grow on its own. Picture a clearing there, if you like. Soft moss underfoot. Cool night air. Moonlight through tall trees. A silver moth landing on your hand, gentle and forgiving, like the breeze.
Nothing grows faster for being pulled. With each breath out, let something in you settle, the way leaves settle on still water.
Nothing to fix here. Nothing to earn. The Dream asks nothing of you, only that you rest in it.
If it's welcome, a wish for yourself. Perhaps: may I rest. May I be at peace. Or whatever words fit better.
And one for someone else out there today. Someone you know, or someone you'll never meet. May they rest too. Everyone is carrying something.
Slowly now, back towards waking. Feel your hands. Perhaps move your fingers, and your shoulders.
When you're ready, open your eyes. Look around, and name one thing you can see.
Andu-falah-dor, thero'shan. Balance restored, a little. The Dream will keep. So will I.
You moved, so we've come back from the Dream. That's alright. It will be here whenever you'd like to return.
Something needs you. Go carefully. The Dream will keep.
Ishnu-alah, thero'shan. Today, let's sit by a moonwell together. Nothing to do well here. And whenever you move, we'll simply come back.
Let your eyes close, or rest softly on one still thing. Let your hands be heavy. Let your weight sink down.
Notice three things you can feel. Where you're sitting. Your feet. The air on your skin. Nothing to change. Just notice.
A moonwell is still water in a ring of old stone. The kaldorei say it holds Elune's light. Picture its surface, quiet and silver.
Breathe in gently, as if smelling a flower by the water. Then let the breath out slowly, as if cooling a cup of tea.
Each breath out sends a ring across the water. Watch it widen, and fade, and the surface grow still again.
If thoughts come, let them be leaves falling on the water. They float. They drift to the edge. You don't have to follow them.
Now think of something small and good from the last few days. A meal. A laugh. A moment of sun. It doesn't have to be much.
Stay with it a while. Where were you? What could you see, or hear? Let it be as clear as it wants to be.
Notice how that feels, somewhere in you. Perhaps a little warmth. Perhaps nothing much. Either is fine.
Good things are easy to rush past. Lingering on one, even for a breath, helps it settle in and stay.
The moonlight is gathering in the well, a little at a time. It never hurries, and it never runs out.
If you'd like, let a little of that light gather in you too. In your chest. In your hands. Quiet, and silver, and enough.
One thing you're thankful for today. Big or small. Just name it to yourself, and let the well hold it.
Nothing to fix here. You're welcome at the water just as you are.
Rest by the well a little longer. I'll keep watch.
Slowly now, come back towards the room. Wriggle your fingers. Roll your shoulders, if you like.
When you're ready, open your eyes. Find one thing nearby that's still, and let your eyes rest on it.
Ishnu-alah, thero'shan. The well will keep your light. Come back to it whenever you like.
And now, the pond. Frogs at the water's edge, singing the evening in. Stay with them as long as you like.
Still again. Let the next breath out take its time. There's no one waiting on it.
Count the leaves moving nearest you, if you like. You are allowed to just watch them move.
Feel the air on your face. Cool, or warm, thero'shan? Just notice which.
The trees have been breathing all day without once thinking about it. You can borrow that.
One long breath out, like blowing on a cup of tea to cool it. Again, if you like.
Look at the farthest thing you can see. Then the nearest. Then let your eyes rest between them.
Your feet, the ground, the roots under the ground. Everything is held up by something. Life is a clockwork made of circles.
Nothing needs deciding right now. The next road can be chosen later.
Let your belly be soft when you breathe in. There's no one here to stand straight for.
Listen to the farthest sound first. Then something closer. Then the closest of all. Listen to your heart.
Stillness isn't empty. Wait a breath or two and watch it fill up.
The light and the shadows, move, very slowly, across the ground. Set your own pace.
If thoughts come, let them pass like travellers on the road. You don't have to walk with them.
The old druids could stand so still that birds would land on them. Butterflies only land on an outstretched hand that waits and miracles only happen when we make space for them.
Let your shoulders drop, then drop a little more. They were carrying more than they needed to.
A leaf doesn't hurry to fall. It drifts. Let the breath out drift like that. You, too, will find the place you are meant to rest.
The ground is warm from the day, or cool from the night. Let yourself feel it. Listen to your feet.
Notice where the breath goes when you breathe in. Let it, and yourself, be.
For a breath or two, nothing to look for. Let the world come to you instead.
The stars are out. Each one was here before the first kaldorei looked up, and will be after.
Night birds, night creatures, night flowers opening. The forest has a second life after dark.
Moonlight makes everything silver and quiet. Even the road looks softer.
Elune's light is a gentle witness. It doesn't ask you to do anything.
The owls are hunting. Their wings make no sound at all. The night is full of quiet skills and unseen miracles. It is enough to know they are there even if we do not see them.
Somewhere a Sentinel is beginning her watch. The night is in good hands.
The moths are out, following the light. Small travellers, guided by the stars, just like us.
Darkness is not something to fear. It is a cloak under which even warriors rest.
The White Lady is full and bright. Her light finds the paths for you.
Shadows under the trees, light between them. Walk slowly, and the night opens up.
The forest is resting now, and so are most of its creatures. Move gently through it.
Dew is gathering on the leaves. By morning, every blade of grass will hold a little moon.
Night has its own colours: deep blue, silver, the faint green of glowing moss. Look for them.
Our people kept the night long before there were walls or cities. You're part of a very old watch.
Nothing to plan here. The road will be there in the morning.
A warm meal, if there's one going. Even a druid needs feeding.
Sit somewhere you can see the door and the fire. Then let your shoulders go.
Resting isn't wasted time. The roots grow most when the leaves are quiet.
The innkeeper has seen a thousand travellers come in tired and leave rested. You're in good hands.
A quiet corner, a warm drink. Simple things, and enough.
Rest well. The forest grows in the dark, too.
Clouds below you, for once. Look how slowly they move.
Hippogryphs have carried our people for a long time. Trust the wings; they know the sky.
Rivers look like silver threads from up here. They all lead to the sea.
Nothing to do but be carried. Rest your hands.
From up here, the forest looks like moss. Every tree, one small green thread.
Somewhere down there, someone is walking the road you walked. Wish them well, if you like.
A long flight is a good time for nothing. Let your thoughts go quiet with the wind.
Mountains, valleys, coastlines. It is the same pattern at distance as it is up close.
The hippogryph's wingbeats are slow and even. Breathe with them, if you like.
Every land you pass over has its own colour. Watch them change.
The water's cool. Feel it around you, and let it hold some of your weight.
Fish don't hurry unless they must. Drift a moment, like they do.
Water finds its way around every stone. It doesn't fight; it just keeps going.
Rivers carry the mountains down to the sea, one grain at a time. Slow, patient work.
Ripples move out from you and fade. Every movement here is gentle and then gone.
The water's edge is busy with life. Reeds, frogs, small fish. Look closely.
Float, if you'd like. Let the water do the holding.
Water remembers where it's been: snow, rain, roots, sea; there are oceans in each drop
A new land. Its trees and stones were here long before the maps.
Look for one thing in this place that you'd want to remember. There's always one.
Every land has creatures that call it home. Let them get used to you.
Somewhere in this land is a quiet spot no one else has found. Keep an eye out.
New paths, new smells, new sounds. Let it be new for a while.
The people here have their own stories. Listen, if you get the chance.
The land here has its own history, written in its rocks and rivers. Read a little of it as you go.
What grows here? What sings here? Every land answers differently.
Ishnu-alah. It's good to have you back on the road.
Welcome back. Take a breath before you begin. The world will wait for that.
Ishnu-alah. The leaves have turned a little while you were away. Come and see.
The roads are where you left them.
Andu-falah-dor. A fresh start, a new day's walking.
Welcome, thero'shan. Whatever you came to do today, I'll be nearby.
Ishnu-alah. Let's go gently.
You came back. The forest noticed.
Good to see you. Where shall the road go today?
Ishnu-alah. Walk gently until next time.
Rest well. The roads will be here.
Elune-adore. Until we walk again.
Good night, thero'shan. The forest keeps its watch.
Sleep, if it's late. Wake to something kind.
Andu-falah-dor. Go well.
Ishnu-alah. Thank you for the company.
Until the next road. I'll be here.
Go gently, wherever you're going.
Another season of growth. Look how far the road reaches behind you now.
You kept walking, even on the slow days. That's how roads get long.
Another step. Take a breath, and notice where you're standing.
Growth is quiet. Most of it happens when no one is watching.
The forest grew a little today, too. You grew along with it.
Another mark on the path. The ones behind you made this one possible.
You stayed curious. The world has a way of opening up for people who keep looking.
One more step up the hill. Turn round and see the view, if you like.
Ishnu-alah. A milestone, and a good place to pause.
Small steps add up. The oak is a majesty of many small multiplied things.
There. Done. Let it be done, for a moment, before the next thing.
Notice what you just did. Not the reward, the doing.
A good piece of work. Let it sit with you a while.
Well done, and no rush to the next. The road will keep.
One more thing set right in the world. Small, and real.
Before you go on, look around. This is where it finished.
A moment's quiet for a job well done. The forest approves.
Something you started is now finished. That's a good feeling. Let it stay.
The task is done. The day goes on, gently.
Rest a breath here. Endings are easy to rush through.
That was done with care. It shows.
A small thing, finished. Small things are most of what the world is made of.
Let it settle. The next road will wait a breath or two.
A small kindness, and the world tilts a little towards good.
Someone's road got easier just now. You may never know how much.
A blessing given freely. Those are the ones that last.
Kindness doesn't need to be thanked to be real.
That stranger will remember light and warmth.
A gift, passed on. Somewhere down the road, it'll be passed on again.
Small mercies add up. Most of the world is held together by them.

Even the Sentinels fall back from a fight that won't turn. Mend first. Choose again after.
When a path keeps closing, druids look for another. Sometimes the way round is the way through.
Each try taught you something about this fight. Gather it up before the next one.
The forest pulls back every winter and doesn't call it defeat. Gather, rest, and return in your own spring.
The enemy will still be there tomorrow. So will you, rested.
Malfurion slept for ages in the Dream before he woke to fight again. A little rest is nothing.
Ishnu-alah. A breath for the road behind, before the road ahead.
Memories settle like fallen leaves. Here's what fell last time.
Before anything new, a look at what's already done.
Looking back isn't standing still. It's how a path becomes yours.
A few lines from last time. Let them come back slowly.
Every journey leaves a shape behind it. Here's the shape of the last one.
Even the oldest trees stop growing each winter. A long day earns a short pause.
Hawks ride the wind instead of beating their wings all day. Find your own wind for a while.
Deer lift their heads between mouthfuls and look around. A long road needs those moments too.
Ishnu-alah, thero'shan. Come and sit beneath an old oak with me for a while. If anything feels wrong, simply move, and we'll come back.
Eyes closed, or resting softly on something low and still. Whichever feels kinder.
High above, the wind moves through the leaves and asks nothing of anyone. Listen to whatever is around you now, near or far. No need to name it.
Now feel where you meet the ground. An oak's roots often reach wider than its branches, holding on in the dark where no one sees. Let the ground hold you the same way.
When you're ready, the breath. In gently. Out a little longer, the way a branch settles after the wind has passed.
Again, in your own time. There's no count to keep. The tree doesn't count its seasons.
Every great oak was once just an acorn seed.
Picture one, small and smooth in its cup, fallen in the autumn grass. Nothing about it looks like a forest.
A jay carries it off and buries it for winter. Jays never find them all. Many oaks stand where a bird forgot.
Before the acorn makes a single leaf, it sends a root down into the cold. The first growing all happens underground, out of sight.
The leaves wait for spring.
Where deer graze, a seedling rarely lasts. But sometimes one comes up inside a bramble patch, and the thorns keep the mouths away.
Foresters have an old saying: the thorn is the mother of the oak. The bramble asks nothing back. In time, the oak will shade it out.
If your mind wanders, that's alright. Notice where it went, and come back to the breath. Each return goes a little deeper.
An oak grows for about forty years before it bears an acorn of its own. Most of its life is simply growing, quietly, ring by ring.
Each year leaves one ring: thin in the hard years, wider in the kind ones. Every ring holds the tree up. It is all of them.
An old oak shelters thousands of other lives: moths, birds, beetles, moss. None of that was the plan when the acorn fell.
And when an oak falls at last, its work isn't over. A stag beetle digs down beside the rotting wood, and lays her eggs in the dark.
Her young live inside that wood for years. Three, five, sometimes seven, slowly turning the old oak back into soil.
Then, one evening in early summer, they climb out. A few weeks of flight in the warm dusk, carried on everything they stored below.
Bramble, oak, beetle. Each one shelters the next, and none of them hurries.
If it's welcome, a few quiet words for yourself. Perhaps: may I grow at my own pace. May I be patient with what's still underground.
And the same wish for someone else. Someone just beginning something, small and uncertain. May they be given time.
Rest beneath the branches a little longer. I'll keep watch.
Slowly now, back towards the room. Feel your feet. Move your fingers, and your shoulders, if you like.
When you're ready, open your eyes, and find one thing nearby that grew once. Wood counts.
Ishnu-alah, thero'shan. Something was planted today. It doesn't need to show yet.
And now, the water below the oak. Frogs, singing the night in. Stay with them as long as you like.
Watch a daisy head over a few days. The outer flowers open first, and the opening moves slowly inward.
The white rays round a daisy's edge make no pollen at all. They're there to be seen.
Turn the head over. That green cup of little leaves holds a whole crowd of flowers together.
The down on a thistle seed was once the flower's sepals. Nothing is wasted; it just becomes something else.
Each tiny floret hands out its pollen a little at a time, and keeps the rest tucked safely inside.
Some daisies open at dawn and close at dusk. They keep the same hours as the light.
A young sunflower follows the sun all day, then turns back east in the dark to wait for morning.
Count the spirals of seed in a sunflower's face, if you like. It's nearly always one of a few numbers: twenty-one, thirty-four, fifty-five.
In damp air a dandelion's parachutes fold shut. Its seeds wait for a dry day before they fly.
Look at a wild rose: five petals on the rim of a little cup. Most of its family are built the same way.
The little cup under the petals holds a ring that makes nectar. That's the gift the bees come for.
Plums, cherries and peaches are all kin of the rose. A whole orchard, from one family.
Apples and pears are rose kin too. Growers have named more than two thousand kinds of apple.
Most of an apple's flesh grows from the flower's cup. Only the core comes from where the seeds were made.
A raspberry comes away hollow; its core stays on the bush. A blackberry brings its core with it.
A bramble's roots live for years, but each cane lives only two: leaves the first year, fruit the second.
A wild rose climbs by hooking its curved prickles over its neighbours. It leans on others, and there's no shame in that.
Birds eat the hips and carry the seeds away, then drop them somewhere new, with a little something to start them growing.
One hawthorn, a thorny cousin of the rose, can feed more than three hundred kinds of insect.
The leaves come in pairs, each pair facing the other across the stem.
The scent lives in tiny oil glands on the leaf hairs. Brush the leaf and they open for you.
The flowers grow in rings around the stem, tier above tier, where the leaves join it.
This family counts more than seven thousand kinds. It's one of the largest in the green world.
Basil, thyme, rosemary and sage are all kin of this one. A good part of a cook's garden is one family.
Most of this family stay small and soft, but a few grow into great hardwood trees.
The sages alone number about a thousand kinds.
Some sages hide a lever inside the flower. A bee pushes in, and a stamen swings down onto the back of its head.
The sage leaves its pollen just where a bee can't groom it off. Patient, and clever.
Mint wanders under the ground on its own stems, and comes up far from where it began.
Roots like this one spend their whole first year as a single leaf of three leaflets. A slow beginning.
You can read a root like this by the scars on its neck, one for every year it has grown.
Roots like this need the shade of trees overhead. In the forest's quiet they take ten years or more to grow.
It makes no seed until it has at least two leaves. There's no rushing a plant like this.
Its berries ripen slowly, six weeks or more, and they aren't ready until they're red all over. Then the birds come.
Its small flowers come in a little umbrella, ten or twenty together, the way the carrot's kin carry theirs.
Ivy is family to this herb. And ivy is no thief; it climbs the tree for light and makes its own food.
Ivy, this herb's cousin, flowers late in the year, when the bees have little else left to visit.
Lotus seeds have woken after more than a thousand years in dry mud. Some things know how to wait.
A lotus seed's shell is waxed outside and lined against water. Nothing gets in.
A lotus breathes like a bellows. Air goes in through the leaves, down to the stem in the mud, and back up again.
A lotus leaf is a whole circle, with no slit cut into it. That's how you tell it from a water lily.
The seed head looks like the rose of a watering can, each seed in its own little hole.
Lotus leaves and seed heads look almost the same in stone a hundred million years old. It found its shape, and kept it.
Its whole family is just two kinds of lotus. A small family, and a very old one.
Run a fingertip up a grass stem. It's hollow between the joints, and solid at each one.
Each grass leaf wraps the stem like a sleeve before it opens out.
A grain is a whole fruit, its wall fused tight to the seed. Every loaf begins like that.
Bamboo is a grass. One has been measured growing more than a metre in a single day.
Some bamboos flower only once in decades, every plant of a kind at once, and then the parents die. One great giving.
Grass roots hold the soil together. Without them the topsoil would wash or blow away.
When fire sweeps a meadow, the grass comes back. Its growing tip waits at the ground, or just below it.
Grass was already growing when the great reptiles walked. Tiny grains of it are in their fossil dung.
A lily bulb is loose fleshy scales with no papery skin. Peel one back and it's like turning pages.
Even one scale broken from a lily bulb can grow new little bulbs along its edge.
Some lilies grow tiny bulbs where leaf meets stem. They drop, and each one can start again.
Look closely: a lily's outer and inner rings look alike. Six matching tepals, not petals and sepals.
Lilies hold their flowers as upright cups, open bowls or hanging bells, each kind in its own way.
A lily's anther is balanced at its back on the tip of its stalk, free to swing.
Mind the pollen. A lily's stains clothes and skin alike.
Flowers of the lily family are often spotted, freckled like a fawn.
A lily's seed pod splits in three when it's ripe, with a hundred or more seeds inside.
Tulips are lily kin. They open in warmth because the inner side of each tepal grows faster than the outer.
This herb's kin are the snowdrops, flowering in late winter while the cold still holds.
A snowdrop hangs its head: three outer petals plain white, three inner ones notched and marked with green.
A snowdrop's leaf tips are hardened like a fingernail, to shield the bud as it pushes up through cold ground.
On a sunny winter day a snowdrop opens in about an hour. A little warmth is enough.
Bees gather more pollen from a hanging snowdrop than from one turned up. Its bow is practical.
Snowdrops spread into clumps, from seed and from new bulbs budding off the old.
After the flowers fade, the leaves keep working, feeding next year's bulb before they rest.
Garlic and daffodils are kin to the snowdrop. One family, from the kitchen to the first flowers of spring.
No plant of this branch makes true wood. Its veins run scattered through the stem, never gathered in a ring.
Their first root dies early and gives way to a tuft of many roots, all much alike.
Palms are kin to grass and lily, and their leaves are the largest of any plant.
A banana plant's trunk isn't a stem at all. It's leaf bases, rolled tight around each other.
Orchids belong to this branch too. Many of them live high on trees, rooted in the bark instead of the soil.
Plants of this branch come up with two seed leaves, side by side.
Hold a leaf like this to the light. Its veins branch into a net, not straight lines like grass.
Cut across a young stem and its veins sit in a neat ring. That ring is what lets a plant make wood.
Most pollen of this branch has three grooves, and botanists name the whole branch for it.
Three-grooved pollen turns up in stone. The oldest found so far is about a hundred and twenty-three million years old.
Most of these plants anchor on one main root, growing straight down from the seedling's first.
Nearly three in every four kinds of flowering plant belong to the heart of this branch.
Long ago an ancestor of these plants copied its whole set of genes three times over. Many still carry the spare flower-building genes.
The richest branch of this family builds nearly every flower on the same five-part plan.
In most of these flowers the green sepals and the coloured petals are clearly two different things.
Some flowers set their parts in a spiral, each one turned the same odd angle, a little over a third of a turn, from the last.
These signs are rules of thumb. The green world always keeps a few exceptions.
There are more than three hundred thousand kinds of flowering plant. Only the insects come in more.
A flower is made of leaves, changed over long ages into petals and all the rest.
A fruit is the wall of a flower's seed chamber, thickened round the growing seeds.
To a botanist, beans and peppers are fruits. Anything that grows from a flower's seed chamber is.
A fruit's work is to keep the seed safe, and then carry it away.
A grain of pollen grows a tube down through the flower to reach the seed within. It carries two sperm cells, not one.
Flowering plants fertilise twice: once for the seed, and once for the food packed round it. No other plants do.
Nearly nine in ten kinds of flowering plant are pollinated by animals: bees, moths, birds and bats.
Bees see colours we can't. Many petals carry marks near the centre that only a bee can see, guiding it in.
Flowers for night moths and bats are often white or very pale. They're made to be found in the dark.
Some plants make nectar away from their flowers, to pay ants to stand guard.
A seed is a young plant packed with food and a coat, able to wait for years. Sometimes thousands.
A seed stays asleep until the ground turns good for growing. It doesn't need to hurry.
Seeds let a plant send its young away, across distance and across time, so they needn't crowd their parent.
A pollen grain is a tiny plant of only a few cells, sealed against drying so it can travel through the air.
Pines and their kin carry their seeds bare on the scales of a cone, not shut away in a fruit.
In spring the pines let go clouds of yellow pollen for the wind to carry.
The soil holds a hidden store of living seeds. Some have waited there for decades.
Most seeds dry out as they ripen. That dryness is what lets them keep.
Water rises in a plant because the leaves breathe it out, pulling a thread of water up behind it.
Up to nine tenths of the water a root drinks goes back into the air from the leaves.
Each root hair is a single cell. Together they give a root far more skin to drink through.
Plants of dry country send their roots deep; plants of wet ground keep them shallow.
On a still, damp night, roots push water up so hard that it beads at the edges of the leaves.
A thin waxy skin covers leaves and stems, so they don't dry out in the open air.
Leaves breathe through tiny pores that open and close, trading a little water for every breath of air.
Every plant on land is descended from a green weed of fresh water.
Plants first came onto land something like five hundred million years ago. Everything green since has followed.
Moss has no true roots, only fine threads that hold on. It drinks through its whole surface instead.
Most moss leaves are only a single cell thick.
A ring of tiny teeth round a moss capsule closes in the wet and opens in the dry, letting spores out on a fine day.
Bog moss can hold more than twenty times its own weight in water.
Moss frozen under ice for fifteen hundred years has been woken and grown again.
An inkcap melts from the rim inward, dripping black ink full of spores. It only begins once the spores are ready.
That black drip from an inkcap really can be used as ink.
An inkcap's stalk can stretch several fingers' breadth in a night, and the whole of it is gone in a few days.
The mushroom is only the fruit. The fungus itself is a web of fine threads through the soil or wood.
A single mushroom can let go more than a billion spores in a day, as fine as smoke.
A mushroom makes its own breeze: water evaporating from the cap cools the air and lifts the spores away.
Lay a cap gills-down on paper overnight, if you like. The spores will leave a print in their own colour.
A fairy ring grows outward from one spore, and the grass on the ring grows darker, fed by what the fungus breaks down.
A mushroom swells with water in a few hours, pushing hard enough to lift a paving stone.
Lichens won't grow where the air is dirty. A rich crop of them means the air here is clean.
Many lichens hold a third partner too: a yeast living in their outer skin. Three lives in one.
Lichens come in three main shapes: flat crusts, leafy sheets and little bushes.
Lichens feed creatures from the very smallest to great herds in the far north.
In the hardest cold a lichen may grow a tenth of a millimetre in a year. It isn't in a hurry.
A fungus's walls are made of chitin, the same tough stuff as a beetle's shell.
A fungus grows only at the very tips of its threads, always reaching outward.
More than a hundred kinds of fungus glow in the dark.
One fungus can spread through the roots and soil of a forest over more than two thousand acres. It's among the largest living things.
Kelp can grow up to a foot and a half in a single day.
Kelp forests hold more kinds of life than almost anywhere else in the sea.
Kelp is brown because a golden pigment hides the green beneath it.
Every great kelp starts as a thread too small to see, which can wait out hard times like a seed in the soil.
Kelp grows from partway along its body, not from the tip.
When plants first came ashore there were no beasts to eat them. Thorns and bitter leaves came later, once the animals followed.
Out of the water, sunlight is harsher. Leaves make their own shade, pigments that soak up the light that burns.
Every spore and pollen grain wears a coat that almost nothing can break down. That's why they last in stone.
At the tip of every shoot is a knot of cells that stays young for the plant's whole life, dividing and dividing.
Every land plant lives two lives in turn: one that makes spores, and one that makes the cells that meet and begin again.
The first plants on land stood only a few fingers high, low green mats all reaching for the same light.
Life on land had its gifts. The sun was brighter, and the air carried a leaf's breath faster than water ever could.
The first green forests filled the air with breath, and made the dry land kinder for the animals that came after.
Moss can dry to a brittle brown mat and wait. When the rain comes, it drinks and turns green again.
A moss spore first grows into a tangle of green threads along the ground. The little leafy stems rise from that later.
A young moss capsule wears a little hood and a lid. Both fall away when the spores inside are ready.
In the coldest lands, moss is much of what grows. Its threads grip the ground without breaking into the frozen soil.
Moss slows the rain from washing soil away, and keeps the small creatures underneath it sheltered.
The veins that carry a plant's water are walled with a tough stuff water can't pass. It's what lets a plant stand tall.
Roots came late. The first plants with veins seem to have had none at all.
Leaves were found more than once. Different branches of the green family flattened their shoots into leaves on their own.
Coal is old forest. Giant club mosses and horsetails once grew in great swamps, and their bodies became the black stone.
A young fern leaf comes up rolled tight, like the head of a fiddle, and slowly unrolls as it grows.
The small club mosses on a forest floor had ancestors that grew into tall trees and made whole swamp forests.
A pine seed can take two years to form after the pollen lands. Some things are worth the wait.
Pine needles are narrow and waxed, so they lose little water. Snow slides off them before a branch can break.
Evergreens keep working quietly through the cold months, so they're ready on the first bright days of spring.
There's a fan-leaved tree that is the last of its whole line. Every close kin it had is gone.
Some old cone-bearers are carried by beetles, not the wind. Their kind grew tall when the great reptiles walked.
One desert plant grows just two leaves in its whole life. They never stop growing, for hundreds of years.
A pine seed holds three generations at once: a coat from the parent tree, a store of food, and the young one itself.
A tree's rings are wide in kind years and narrow in hard ones. Read them and you read the weather of its life.
Tiny seeds often wait for light before they sprout, so they only start near the surface, where the sun can reach them in time.
Many seeds need a winter's cold before they'll sprout. A warm spell in the dark months won't fool them.
On a pine the seed cones sit high and the pollen cones low, so a tree's own pollen rarely drifts onto its own seeds.
Some pines live more than four thousand years, and are still growing.
Deep in every root is a waxed gate. Water must pass through living cells there, and most poisons are turned away.
Lay a plant on its side and within hours it turns upward again. Grains of starch settle in its cells to show which way is down.
Look where each leaf meets the stem. A small bud waits there, ready to become a branch or a flower.
In poor, boggy ground some flowering plants catch insects, to get the goodness the soil can't give them.
Feel the fine hairs on a leaf. They slow crawling insects, hold bitter juices, and keep the drying wind off.
A tendril coils at the lightest touch. The side that meets the support shrinks, and the far side grows.
Bees can't see red. The flowers that want bees mostly wear blues and yellows instead.
Some flowers smell of rot on purpose, and wear dull browns and purples. They're calling the flies.
Flowers that wait for birds are often bright and tube-shaped, and they hardly smell at all.
Flowers that trust the wind are small and green, with no nectar or scent. Many open before the leaves, so nothing blocks the breeze.
Many flowers can tell their own pollen from a stranger's, and quietly turn their own away.
In some flowers the pollen and the seed-cup ripen at different times, so a flower can't pollinate itself.
A pollen tube doesn't wander. It follows a scent laid by two small helper cells beside the egg.
A squirrel's forgotten store can become a grove. Buried fruit, never found again, may sprout come spring.
Many plants know the season by the length of the night. When the dark grows long, some of them choose to flower.
A ripening fruit breathes out a gas that hurries its neighbours along. Lay an unripe one beside it and watch.
When a caterpillar chews some leaves, the plant gives off a scent that calls in the caterpillar's hunters.
Before a leaf falls, the plant takes back what it can. The yellow is the green being packed away for later.
The green cups beneath a flower are its sepals. They wrapped the bud and kept it safe before it opened.
Some fruits split open to let their seeds go, like a pea pod. Others, like a peach, wait to soften and fall apart.
Just under a leaf's skin, cells stand packed in columns, like a fence of stakes, catching the light first.
Beneath the columns, the leaf's cells sit loose with air between them, so the leaf can breathe.
Cut across a young root of this branch and the strands that carry its water make a cross, an X at the very centre.
Flax is of this branch. Linen is spun from the long fibres in its stem, cells stiffened with the stuff of wood.
A potato is a swollen underground stem. Its eyes are buds, each ready to grow a new shoot.
Inside a forming seed of this branch, the young plant is shaped like a tiny heart, its two seed leaves just beginning.
A seedling of this branch pushes up bent like a crook, guarding its tender tip. In the light it straightens.
Split a pea in two. Each half is a seed leaf, packed with food for the seedling.
In many seedlings of this branch the stem below the seed leaves stretches up, and lifts them into the light.
A seed of this branch wears two coats, a tough outer one and a thin one within.
Primroses grow in two forms, long-styled and short. A bee drinking from one carries pollen to the other.
Some orchids offer bright colour and sweet scent, but no nectar at all. The bee leaves hungry, carrying pollen.
Orchids alone count more than twenty-five thousand kinds, all of them kin to grass and lily.
The yucca keeps a single moth for a partner. The moth carries its pollen, and the moth's young eat a few of its seeds.
A grass shoot comes up inside a closed sheath that guards its first leaf. Once it meets the light, the sheath stops growing.
Each strand of silk on an ear of corn is a flower's own pollen-catcher. Every kernel is a seed.
Bite a pear and feel the grit. Those are tiny stone cells, their walls hardened like wood.
Strawberries send runners along the ground. Each one roots where it touches and starts a new plant.
A rose leaf is small leaflets set along a stalk, in pairs, like the barbs of a feather.
A raspberry is many tiny fruits from a single flower, all holding together as one.
Garden roses are often grafted, one rose's stem set on another's roots. In time their veins join and they grow as one.
Pull a dandelion and the long root usually snaps. What's left in the ground grows a fresh shoot.
Every land plant stores its food as starch, the same way its green ancestors in the water did.
The cells of a land plant are joined by tiny channels through their walls, so each can pass things to its neighbour.
The green in this leaf is the same pair of pigments its far-off ancestors used in fresh water.
Fungi reached the land before plants did. The first green things to come ashore already had fungi living inside them.
A fungus eats the other way round from us. It pours its digestion out into the wood first, then drinks in what's left.
A fungus stores its food the way animals do, not as starch the way plants do.
Where the soil is poor, some fungi hunt. They set little rings in their threads that swell shut on passing worms.
An orchid seed carries almost no food of its own. It won't sprout at all unless a fungus feeds it.
Some ants keep gardens. They carry cut leaves underground for a fungus to eat, and then they eat the fungus.
Look for powdery specks on a lichen. Each is a few green cells wrapped in fungus thread, waiting for wind or rain to carry it.
Weavers once dyed their wool with lichens. The colours were waiting in the crust all along.
Neither partner in a lichen can usually live alone. The fungus gives shelter, and the green cells give food.
Cut a lichen through and you'd find layers: a tough skin of fungus on top, then a thin green band where the light is caught.
Each gill is packed threads, lined with tiny clubs. Every club makes four spores, set out on four little stalks.
In the threads of a mushroom, each cell carries two nuclei, one from each parent, side by side. They only join just before the spores are made.
The brightest red caps, flecked with white, are poison. Here the beauty is a warning.
Each spore is flung from the gill by a drop of water. It gathers at the spore's base, then snaps across it, and the spore is away.
A spore is thrown only a hair's breadth, just far enough to clear its gill without striking the one facing it.
Sea otters wrap themselves in kelp to sleep, so the tide can't carry them away.
Kelp grows only in cool, rich water near the shore, and never deeper than the light can follow.
Winter storms leave a kelp forest torn and ragged. Each spring it begins to grow again.
Early in the morning, tiny swellings inside each grass flower push it open. Then the stamens slip out to dangle in the wind.
Some grass seeds carry a twisted bristle. As the air dries and dampens, it turns and screws the seed down into the soil.
Grass feeds most of the world. Bread, rice and corn are all its seeds, and the herds eat it too.
Where a grass blade leaves its stem, look for a small flap. It keeps dirt and pests out of the sleeve.
A leaf of this branch grows from its base, pushing its older tip ahead of it, longer but hardly wider.
Many plants of this branch keep their growing tips underground, safe from frost, fire and hungry mouths.
A palm trunk reaches its full thickness while it's young, right at the growing tip, and hardly widens after.
This family grows on every land but the frozen far south. Few families have wandered so widely.
What we call a sunflower seed is really a whole fruit. Crack the shell and the true seed is inside.
An artichoke is a flower head of this family, picked and eaten as a bud before it can open.
Goldenrod is daisy kin. Its pollen is rich enough to help the bees through the winter.
Some chrysanthemums make their own poison against insects. Folk have long used it to keep pests away.
Not every daisy kin calls the bees. Ragweed gives its pollen to the wind, and sets autumn noses running.
Growers have named more than five thousand kinds of garden rose.
Look at the base of a rose's leaf stalk. Two small wings of leaf usually hug the stem there.
The pips and stones of rose-kin fruits carry a bitter defence. Better to spit them out than chew them.
Catmint draws cats by its strong scent. Some grow sleepy on it, and others turn wild.
Lavender is kin to this herb. In summer its flowers draw bees like lantern light draws moths.
Lavender's scent isn't only in its flowers. Rub the grey leaves and you'll find the oil there too.
Lamb's ear is mint kin too. Its leaves are so thick with fine hairs they feel like felt.
Each flower of this family leaves behind four small hard nutlets, its seeds.
Look inside one of these flowers: often four stamens, one pair longer than the other.
Catmint's nectar sits deep in a narrow tube, so it's mostly the long-tongued bees that come to drink.
Breathe in a crushed mint leaf. The cool you feel isn't cold at all; its oil wakes the nerves that sense cold.
Ivy lives two lives. Young, it climbs and never flowers. Grown, it stops climbing and blooms.
Ivy's berries ripen blue-black. They are poison to us, so leave them for the birds.
Each red berry of a root like this holds only two or three pale seeds.
Look at the leaves of a grown plant: a ring of three, each spread open like a hand.
A seed of this root sleeps a year and a half before it will sprout. Patience is built into it.
A daffodil's trumpet is a crown grown from the throat of the flower, ringed by six spreading petals.
Daffodils turn their faces to follow the sun.
Deer and rabbits leave daffodils alone. Every part is bitter with poison, the bulb most of all.
Daffodil sap carries tiny crystals shaped like needles. Hands that pick many flowers can itch from them.
Leave an onion to flower and it sends up a round cluster of small white stars.
Tulips are lily kin, and they come in every colour but a true blue.
Look inside a tulip. Its anthers are most often black.
A tulip's seed pod holds flat seeds stacked in rows, like little coins.
Tulip petals taste mild, a little like fresh peas. The bulb is another matter.
Lily seeds pack their food as oil, not starch.
Keep cats away from lilies. Every part is poison to them, even the pollen.
A lotus flower lasts about three days. It opens each morning and closes again each night.
When the seed head ripens it breaks off and floats away, dropping its seeds as it slowly comes apart.
Beetles and bees carry a lotus's pollen from one great flower to the next.
A lotus flower can open wider than two spread hands.
A lotus spreads by thick stems creeping through the mud, until it can fill a whole pond.
Nearly every part of a lotus can feed someone: the young leaves, the thick roots, the seeds.
Roses, cabbages, sunflowers and mints all belong to this one great branch.
Sugar comes from two plants: a tall grass, and a beet of this branch.
This branch holds soft little herbs and great hardwood trees alike.
Acorns are bitter on purpose. They're packed with things that put off hungry mouths.
An early flower of this branch, pressed in stone more than a hundred million years ago, looks much like a buttercup.
Buttercups and poppies sit near the root of this branch, sister to all the rest of it.
In a tomato seed the food lies outside the seed leaves. When it wakes, the two leaves drink it in.
Ishnu-alah, thero'shan. Come and sit by a small fire with me for a while. If anything feels wrong, simply move, and we'll come back.
Eyes closed, or resting softly on the glow, or on something low and still. Whichever feels kinder.
A fire is never quite silent. Listen to whatever is around you now, the near sounds and the far ones. No need to name them.
Warmth on the side that faces the fire. Beneath, the ground, cooler and steady, holding everything up.
When you're ready, the breath. In gently. Out slowly, too softly to stir the ash.
Again, in your own time. A fire breathes too: it takes the air it needs, and no more.
Above, the leaves are turning, ember-red and gold. One lets go, and drifts down past the firelight.
A leaf doesn't fall from weakness. The tree draws back what it can use, seals the stem, and lets it go.
On the ground, fungi and worms slowly turn the leaves to soil. Next year's growing is made from this year's letting go.
If your mind wanders, that's alright. Thoughts drift like sparks. Watch where one goes, then come back to the warmth.
Somewhere under the leaves, poppy seeds are waiting, each no bigger than a pinhead.
A single poppy can scatter tens of thousands of them. Most don't grow that year. They wait.
A fresh seed isn't ready yet. It needs months in the soil first, resting in the dark, before it can wake at all.
And then it can wait for years. Decades, some of them, until the ground is turned and light finally reaches them.
Where a field is ploughed, or a bank slips, poppies are often the first colour back. They were there all along.
There is a kind of poppy that waits for fire. Its seeds lie still for years, until the smoke of a burned hillside tells them it's time.
After the fire, the ash is rich and the light comes down through the open canopy. The poppies bloom where the old growth stood.
Ember, leaf and seed. Each one is something ending and something waiting, both at once.
A few quiet words for yourself, said or only thought. May I rest while I wait. May I be ready when the light comes.
And the same wish for someone else. Perhaps someone met on the road, whose name stayed with you. May their fire stay warm.
The fire is low now, a bed of red embers. Embers hold their heat long after the flames are gone.
Rest by the embers a little longer. I'll keep watch.
Slowly now, back towards the room. Feel your hands. Move your fingers, then your shoulders.
When you're ready, open your eyes, and find one warm colour nearby. Let your eyes rest on it.
Ishnu-alah, thero'shan. The embers will keep. So will the seeds.
And now, past the firelight, frogs are singing at the water's edge. Stay with them a while.
